traits: Smooth gray trunk, sometimes with a slight bulge partway up, ringed with old leaf-scar marks
Long, gracefully arching feather fronds with dark green leaflets
Large hanging clusters of small round orange fruit, sometimes over a thousand per cluster
No true crownshaft — new fronds emerge without a smooth green tube at the top of the trunk

look_alikes.difference: Queen palm leaflets droop in loose, irregular groups, no crownshaft; foxtail leaflets radiate stiffly all around the rib like a bottlebrush.
look_alikes.next_photo: A wide shot of the whole crown showing frond shape, plus a close-up of the trunk top for a crownshaft.

look_alikes.difference: Queen palm has small round orange fruit in huge clusters and a slender trunk; coconut palm has large coconuts and a thicker, often curved trunk.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the fruit size and color, plus a wide shot of the trunk shape.

copy.what_it_means: A fast-growing, widely planted landscape palm known for its graceful arching fronds. It's prone to several nutrient deficiencies, especially on Southwest Florida's alkaline soils, and a technician can tell a nutrition issue apart from a more serious trunk disease by which fronds are affected and how.
copy.fact: A single queen palm fruit cluster can carry more than a thousand seeds, which is why the fruit drop under one can be a real cleanup job.
copy.blurb: A fast-growing, gracefully arching landscape palm, prone to nutrient deficiencies on Southwest Florida's alkaline soils.

tech_notes: Prone to potassium, manganese, iron and boron deficiencies; distinguish nutrition issues from Fusarium wilt (one-sided frond death, reddish-brown petiole stripe) and Ganoderma butt rot (trunk conks) before recommending any nutrition correction, which stays within the local fertilizer rules.

id_cues: Smooth gray trunk, sometimes slightly bulging, with visible ring scars
No crownshaft — new fronds emerge directly from the trunk top
Long, arching feather fronds
Huge hanging clusters of small round orange fruit
plant.frond_pattern_note: Potassium deficiency shows first on the oldest, lowest fronds; manganese and boron problems show on the newest; fusarium kills one side of a frond at a time.

traits: Leaflets grow whorled all the way around the frond's central rib, giving each frond a bushy, fox-tail look
Light gray to nearly white trunk, often slightly swollen mid-way up
Smooth, pale to blue-green crownshaft at the top of the trunk
Egg-shaped fruit that ripens from green to orange-red just below the crownshaft

look_alikes.difference: Foxtail leaflets radiate stiffly around the rib like a bottlebrush, with a crownshaft; queen palm leaflets droop in loose, irregular groups, no crownshaft.
look_alikes.next_photo: A wide shot of the whole crown showing frond shape, plus a close-up of the trunk top for a crownshaft.

look_alikes.difference: Foxtail palm has bushy, whorled leaflets and a slender trunk; royal palm has plain flat fronds, a much thicker gray trunk, and grows far taller.
look_alikes.next_photo: A wide shot comparing overall height and trunk thickness, plus a close-up of the frond/leaflet arrangement.

look_alikes.difference: Foxtail palm has a smooth crownshaft and bushy whorled leaflets; coconut palm has no crownshaft, a curved trunk, and large coconuts, not small orange fruit.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the trunk top for a crownshaft, plus a wide shot of the fruit size.

copy.what_it_means: A popular landscape palm named for its bushy, fox-tail-shaped fronds. Overhead irrigation hitting the fronds can encourage a fungal leaf spot, so a technician checks watering pattern along with the leaves themselves before recommending anything.
copy.fact: Its leaflets grow whorled all the way around the frond's central rib rather than lying flat in one plane, which is exactly what gives each frond its bushy, tail-like look.
copy.blurb: A landscape palm named for its bushy, fox-tail-shaped fronds — overhead watering can invite a leaf spot fungus.

tech_notes: Leaf spot fungus can worsen with overhead irrigation hitting the foliage; recommend base watering. Ganoderma butt rot is a trunk-level concern requiring closer inspection.

review.notes: The full nutrient-deficiency profile (manganese, boron) commonly cited for foxtail palm in horticultural sources is not confirmed on a UF/IFAS page opened in this pass; potassium deficiency was added to common_problems as a reasonable, lower-confidence addition.

id_cues: Leaflets whorled around the frond's rib, giving a bushy, fox-tail look
Light gray to whitish trunk, sometimes slightly swollen mid-way up
Smooth, pale to blue-green crownshaft
Egg-shaped fruit ripening orange-red just below the crownshaft
plant.frond_pattern_note: Leaf spot fungus can appear on any frond, especially with overhead watering; potassium deficiency starts on the oldest fronds; Ganoderma affects the trunk, not one frond.

traits: Tall, smooth, light gray trunk, sometimes with a slight bulge, up to two feet across
Bright green crownshaft, roughly five feet tall, sitting cleanly above the trunk
Large, plain, flat feather fronds, ten to fifteen feet long
Sheds one whole dead frond at a time on its own (self-cleaning) rather than holding dead fronds

look_alikes.difference: Royal palm is a much taller tree with plain flat fronds and a thick gray trunk; foxtail palm is smaller and slender with bushy, whorled 'foxtail' leaflets.
look_alikes.next_photo: A wide shot comparing overall height and trunk thickness, plus a close-up of the frond/leaflet arrangement.

look_alikes.difference: Royal palm is a large tree with a thick trunk and a tall green crownshaft; Christmas palm stays small, with a thin trunk and red holiday fruit.
look_alikes.next_photo: A wide shot comparing overall size, plus a close-up of the fruit color if present.

copy.what_it_means: A tall, stately palm and a Florida landscape icon, known for dropping one whole dead frond at a time on its own rather than needing regular trimming. Its size means a falling frond can be genuinely heavy, and a technician checks the crown and trunk before recommending any work at height.
copy.fact: It drops its dead fronds cleanly on its own about once a month, but each one can weigh up to 50 pounds fresh, so a falling frond is a real hazard, not just a mess.
copy.blurb: A tall Florida landscape icon that self-cleans its own dead fronds — impressive, but a falling frond is genuinely heavy.

tech_notes: A tapering, 'pencil-pointing' trunk points to advanced potassium deficiency rather than normal growth. Royal palm bug damage is confined to the newest, still-folded fronds. Ganoderma and Thielaviopsis are trunk-level, specialist-referral concerns.

id_cues: Bright green crownshaft, roughly five feet tall, above a smooth gray trunk
Large, plain, flat feather fronds with no whorled or bushy look
Sheds one whole dead frond cleanly on its own each month
Grows much taller than most landscape palms, up to 50-70 feet
plant.frond_pattern_note: Potassium deficiency shows on the oldest fronds; royal palm bug damage appears only in the newest, still-folded fronds near the top.

traits: Fan-shaped (costapalmate) fronds split only about a third of the way to the base, with long thread-like fibers between segments
Trunk often still wearing old, crisscrossed leaf bases called 'boots,' especially on younger palms
Rounded, full canopy of many fronds rather than a sparse crown
Florida's state tree — the most common native palm in the landscape

look_alikes.difference: Cabbage palm has a rougher, often boot-covered trunk and fronds split partway with thread fibers; Chinese fan palm has a smoother trunk, drooping frond tips.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the trunk (boots present or smooth) and the frond segment tips (stiff vs. drooping).

copy.what_it_means: Florida's state tree and the most common native palm in the landscape, tough and low-maintenance under normal conditions. Lethal bronzing is the serious concern to rule out on this species, so a technician looks at which fronds are affected and how the decline is progressing before saying more.
copy.fact: The palm's old leaf bases, called 'boots,' often host other plants living in the crevices — ferns, air plants, even a strangler fig seedling can get its start there.
copy.blurb: Florida's state tree and toughest common native palm — lethal bronzing is the main serious concern to rule out.

tech_notes: Lethal bronzing is the priority differential on this species; confirm frond-position pattern (oldest first, moving up) and check for premature fruit drop or spear leaf death before any referral. Salt in the root zone (not spray) stresses this species despite its toughness.

id_cues: Fan-shaped fronds split only a third of the way to the base, with thread-like fibers between segments
Trunk often still covered in old crisscrossed leaf-base 'boots'
Full, rounded canopy rather than a sparse crown
Very common as a native, unplanted volunteer as well as a landscape tree
plant.frond_pattern_note: Lethal bronzing and potassium deficiency start on the oldest, lowest fronds; Ganoderma affects the trunk; palmetto weevil attacks the crown, especially on transplants.

traits: Smooth, light grayish-brown trunk that is often distinctly curved or leaning, sometimes with a swollen base
Very large arching fronds, up to 18 feet long
Large, green-husked coconuts, often a foot or more long, hanging in clusters below the crown
No crownshaft — new fronds emerge directly from the trunk top

look_alikes.difference: Coconut palm has large coconuts and a thicker, often curved trunk; queen palm has small round orange fruit in huge clusters and a slender, straighter trunk.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the fruit size and color, plus a wide shot of the trunk shape.

look_alikes.difference: Coconut palm has no crownshaft, a curved trunk, and large coconuts; foxtail palm has a smooth blue-green crownshaft and small orange-red egg-shaped fruit.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the trunk top for a crownshaft, plus a wide shot of the fruit size.

copy.what_it_means: A coastal icon whose most serious threat is lethal yellowing, a disease that has no cure and typically kills the palm within months once yellowing sets in. A photo alone can't rule it out, so any yellowing that starts on the oldest fronds alongside dropping fruit is worth a closer look.
copy.fact: Lethal yellowing often shows up first as premature fruit drop and blackened flower stalks, before the fronds themselves ever turn yellow.
copy.blurb: A coastal icon whose main threat, lethal yellowing, has no cure — early fruit drop is often the first sign.

tech_notes: Lethal yellowing progresses from the oldest fronds upward with premature fruit drop and blackened inflorescences; there is no cure once advanced, only preventive trunk injection for nearby palms. Confirm before any customer conversation about removal.

id_cues: Trunk is often distinctly curved or leaning, sometimes with a swollen base
No crownshaft — fronds emerge directly from the trunk top
Very large, arching fronds up to 18 feet long
Large green-husked coconuts hanging in clusters
plant.frond_pattern_note: Lethal yellowing, lethal bronzing and potassium deficiency all start on the oldest fronds; boron deficiency shows on the newest fronds; Ganoderma affects the trunk.

traits: Multiple slender stems (2-3 inches thick) clustered together from the base rather than one single trunk
Tightly packed rings on each stem, ranging from orange-yellow to dark green depending on sun exposure
Yellowish-green, gently arching feather fronds
Often planted and pruned as a dense privacy screen or accent clump

look_alikes.difference: Areca palm grows as a dense clump of many slender, ringed stems, no single trunk; Christmas palm has one curving trunk with red holiday fruit.
look_alikes.next_photo: A wide shot of the base — multiple clustered stems (areca) vs. one single trunk (Christmas palm).

copy.what_it_means: A popular clustering palm used for screening and accent plantings, made up of many slender stems rather than one trunk. Some yellowing of the lowest fronds is a normal part of its growth, but wider yellowing across the clump is worth a closer look, since it can point to a nutrient issue.
copy.fact: Every new shoot that emerges from the base starts out crumpled looking before it unfolds, which can look alarming even though it's completely normal for this species.
copy.blurb: A popular clustering privacy-screen palm — some lower-frond yellowing is normal, but wider yellowing is worth a look.

tech_notes: Distinguish normal age-related lower-frond yellowing from a nutrient deficiency or spider mite stippling before recommending anything; prune lower fronds mainly to reduce pest/fungus harborage in the stem cluster.

review.notes: Potassium/manganese deficiency and spider mite susceptibility are well documented for areca palm in general horticultural sources but not spelled out on the UF/IFAS pages opened in this pass.

id_cues: Multiple slender stems clustered together, not one single trunk
Tightly packed rings on each stem, orange-yellow to dark green
Yellowish-green, gently arching fronds
New shoots look crumpled before unfolding — normal, not damage
plant.frond_pattern_note: Potassium deficiency shows first on the oldest fronds; manganese deficiency on the newest; spider mite stippling can appear on any frond in dry conditions.

traits: Single, gently curving, slender trunk, usually 5-6 inches thick, often planted in small clumps of 2-4

copy.what_it_means: A popular small landscape palm named for its clusters of bright red fruit that ripen around the holidays. Lethal yellowing is the serious disease to rule out on this species, so a technician looks at which fronds are affected before saying more.
copy.fact: Its bright red fruit clusters ripen right around the holiday season, which is exactly where the common name "Christmas palm" comes from.
copy.blurb: A popular small landscape palm whose red fruit ripens right around the holidays.

tech_notes: Lethal yellowing progresses from the oldest fronds upward; Ganoderma butt rot is a trunk-level, specialist-referral concern. Confirm frond pattern before any conversation about removal.

copy.what_it_means: A small, popular accent palm, often planted in clusters near entryways and pools. It's prone to several nutrient deficiencies typical of palms, and a technician can tell those apart from a more serious leaf spot or trunk disease by which fronds are affected.

copy.blurb: A small, popular accent palm often clustered near entryways — its lower leaflets are sharp spines, not soft foliage.

tech_notes: Prone to potassium, manganese and boron deficiencies plus Pestalotiopsis leaf spot; distinguish from Ganoderma butt rot (trunk-level, specialist referral) before recommending any nutrition correction, which stays within the local fertilizer rules.

traits: Massive, thick trunk, 2-3 feet across, with an attractive diamond-shaped pattern of old leaf scars

copy.what_it_means: A massive, statement landscape palm valued for its imposing diamond-patterned trunk. Fusarium wilt is the serious disease to watch for, spread mainly on pruning tools, so a technician looks at which side of a frond is affected before saying more.

copy.blurb: A massive, statement palm known for its diamond-patterned trunk — Fusarium wilt is the serious disease to watch for.

tech_notes: Fusarium wilt spreads mainly via contaminated pruning tools — disinfect between palms. Graphiola false smut on the oldest fronds is cosmetic and often doesn't warrant treatment in a landscape setting.

copy.what_it_means: A slow-growing fan palm valued for its graceful, drooping frond tips, sometimes called the fountain palm for that reason. Potassium deficiency is its most common issue, and a technician can tell that apart from a more serious disease by which fronds show it.

copy.blurb: A slow-growing fan palm with gracefully drooping frond tips, sometimes called the fountain palm.

copy.what_it_means: A very tall, fast-growing fan palm commonly used as a street or skyline tree, known for its strongly tapering trunk. A dead frond skirt is mostly a fire and appearance concern rather than a health issue, but a technician still checks the crown for signs of disease.
